cards.headline: Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war

pages.text: Confidential data from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, analyzed by the Guardian, reveals that more than 1,000 Russian soldiers have been recorded as having died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Analysts say this figure almost certainly underestimates the true number of suicides. An additional 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as having died from firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent,” a classification experts say can conceal suicides. Combined, these figures amount to approximately a Russian regiment of dead. The data provides a previously unreported glimpse into the strain on Russia’s armed forces during a war characterized by heavy losses and harsh discipline.

cards.headline: COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, ends without agreement on fossil fuel text

pages.text: Negotiations at the COP31 global climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, concluded two days after the scheduled finish without reaching an agreement. The talks ended after the European Union led a revolt that prevented the consensus required to adopt a proposed cover text. The primary sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in the draft texts. For many observers, the ability of countries to make headway on fossil fuels—the root cause of climate change—was the litmus test for the summit's success.

While some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text indicates the entire summit was a failure, the failure of these texts does not signal the end of the COP process or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. These political, overarching statements have functioned as add-ons to the formal negotiation process since the Glasgow meeting in 2021 and are not a requirement for the process. However, the lack of agreement may mean that international climate cooperation will look different moving forward. The EU and other nations stated that the international process did not meet the moment during a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño, and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming.

cards.headline: US Treasury sanctions more than two dozen Iranian entities to disrupt shadow banking networks

pages.text: The US Department of the Treasury announced on November 23, 2026, that it has sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. The move is part of Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign intended to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks. The Treasury claims these entities help Iran move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent described the shadow banking system as the “last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.” According to a Treasury statement, the Central Bank of Iran oversees the designated entities. The US Treasury claimed its sanctions campaign has pushed the Iranian rial to new lows and driven inflation to approximately 90 percent.

Among the designated entities is the Iran-based Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan). The Treasury claims Nesim Baharan worked closely with Iranian exchange houses and front companies to facilitate transactions for Sarmayeh Bank’s Iranian clients, including major Iranian petrochemical companies. Other sanctioned entities include Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company, along with a number of their owners and employees. These sanctions come amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to end the nine-month US-Israel war on Iran. While Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated that Tehran still hopes diplomacy can end the war, US President Donald Trump said Iran wants a deal that is not acceptable to him. Trump told a Fox News chief foreign correspondent that he is “inclined to order military strikes against Iran after the new year if the two countries fail to reach an agreement.”

cards.headline: UK sanctions five Myanmar military leaders following ICJ genocide ruling

pages.text: The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on five senior Myanmar military leaders following a ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. On November 23, 2026, the UK announced the measures, which include asset freezes, travel bans, and director disqualifications for Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe, and Kyaw Swar Oo. These officers are suspected of involvement in the repression of civilian populations and other serious human rights abuses in Myanmar. This follows a November 19, 2026, ICJ verdict which determined that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the evidence. This ruling marked the first time in the 80-year history of the ICJ that a state has been found guilty of genocide.

The sanctions and legal actions follow a 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar that killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 people to flee the Buddhist-majority country. The ICJ found that Myanmar committed genocide during these military operations in Rakhine state. In response to the ruling, the UK expelled Myanmar's defence attaché and announced plans for new legislation to stop the supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar to address the military's continued airstrikes on civilians. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband stated that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is directly responsible for many of the atrocities as he was the head of the military during the 2017 genocide. Miliband called for an immediate pause in hostilities, a stop to airstrikes on civilians, the release of political prisoners, and dialogue toward an inclusive political settlement.

The UK is among 14 countries that have acknowledged the ICJ ruling. In a joint statement on November 23, 2026, the foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia, and the United Kingdom stated that Myanmar had violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention. The UK also announced a package of humanitarian and justice-related funding: £5 million in additional assistance to support approximately 350,000 people in Rakhine state with essential services, and up to £3 million to strengthen accountability and justice for survivors. This includes supporting the collection of evidence and doubling support for the UN’s International Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM). Myanmar's government has called the ICJ ruling unfair and a “great disappointment.”

cards.headline: Quebec court mandates oath to King, suspending law that made allegiance optional

pages.text: A Quebec Superior Court judge has suspended a provincial law that made the oath to King Charles optional, ruling that members of the National Assembly must swear allegiance before sitting. Justice Ian Demers ordered the suspension after determining that the Quebec government overstepped its constitutional boundaries with its 2022 law. The ruling creates uncertainty for the National Assembly's planned Dec. 1 start date and could lead to a major constitutional battle. Demers warned that laws passed at the National Assembly could be rendered invalid if members do not take the oath, writing that the Constitution is not an “à la carte menu from which an individual subject to its authority may choose to follow only what suits them.”

The 2022 law was passed unanimously by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government led by François Legault, following pressure from the Parti Québécois, which was in opposition at the time. Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who has vowed to abolish the monarchy in Quebec, said his government will appeal the decision. St-Pierre Plamondon, who previously stated during an election campaign that a PQ government would defund the office of Quebec's lieutenant-governor and abolish the monarchy in Quebec, said at a Montreal news conference that he will consider all legal and political options to respect democracy. He stated, “I cannot take an oath to the King of England. And I think we are dozens and maybe more than 100 elected members of parliament duly elected through a democratic process who think it's a disgrace.”

The decision follows several delays for the parliamentary session, which was initially scheduled to begin on Nov. 17 before being pushed back to Nov. 24 and then to the beginning of December. Other political figures have responded to the ruling: Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime expressed hope the decision could be overturned by the Court of Appeal, stating that members' first loyalty is to the people of Quebec. Charles Milliard, head of the Opposition Quebec Liberals, called for the National Assembly to resume sitting, while the leader of the Quebec Conservatives and several former CAQ ministers also said the province should challenge the ruling.

cards.headline: Colombia's repeal of Amazon mining and oil ban draws expert warnings

pages.text: The Colombian government, led by President Abelardo De la Espriella, has repealed Resolution 0961, a measure that prohibited large-scale mining and hydrocarbon extraction in the Amazon region. Experts warn the decision weakens protections for the biome and the Indigenous peoples who sustain it. While the resolution was not the only measure protecting the Amazon, civil society organizations described it as an important complementary measure that marked the first time a country had moved to declare the Amazon biome a zone free of extractive industries. Raphael Hoetmer, director of Amazon Watch’s Western Amazon Program, stated the repeal can be seen as an endorsement of efforts to advance oil and mining projects in the region, noting that while the measure may not have been entirely effective as a protection, the repeal is politically important.

The Ministry of Environment argued the resolution was repealed because it was enacted without prior consultation with the region’s Afro-Colombian, Raizal, and Palenquero traditional communities. Authorities also characterized the resolution as an “administrative act” that created “economic and territorial uncertainty.” In a video shared on social media in November 2026, Colombian Environment Minister Fabio Arjona argued that Amazon protection did not begin with the resolution issued by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro, stating that a large percentage of the Amazon is covered by protection measures because it lies within Indigenous territories and national parks.

The repealed resolution had ordered the protection of more than 48 million hectares (118.6 million acres) of the Amazon from new large-scale mining and fossil fuel extraction. A 2025 report by Earth Insight, the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD), and the National Organization of Indigenous Peoples of the Colombian Amazon (OPIAC) warned that 14 million hectares (34.6 million acres) of oil and gas blocks cover 28% of the Colombian Amazon, with 8 million hectares (19.8 million acres) overlapping intact forests. Organizations noted that fossil fuel extraction and its infrastructure have accelerated forest loss in the Colombian Amazon, which can pave the way for other industries such as logging, mining, and agriculture.

cards.headline: Syria reports progress in eliminating former regime's chemical weapons

pages.text: Syria has announced progress in eliminating the chemical weapons legacy of its deposed regime, providing more than 100,000 pages of documents to international inspectors. Addressing the 31st Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention in The Hague, Syria's Minister of Emergency and Disaster Management Raed al-Saleh stated that the country has facilitated witness interviews and granted access to military facilities and other sites that were previously inaccessible to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW). The OPCW is the international body responsible for implementing the Chemical Weapons Convention, a treaty aimed at prohibiting the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons. Al-Saleh said the new Syrian government has committed to full cooperation with the OPCW, a position reaffirmed during a visit to Damascus by OPCW Director-General Fernando Arias and his meeting with President Ahmad al-Sharaa.

The minister noted that the fall of the deposed regime nearly two years ago helped address a chemical weapons program that had remained unresolved for more than a decade. Al-Saleh said the issue had reached a near deadlock before the Syrian revolution succeeded in overthrowing the deposed regime. He stated that Syria's cooperation has assisted investigators in establishing a clearer picture of the former regime's chemical weapons activities and advancing efforts to identify and eliminate remaining stockpiles and related materials. Al-Saleh also recalled chemical weapons attacks in Ghouta, Moadamiya, Douma, Khan Sheikhoun, Sarmin, Latamneh, and other Syrian towns and cities.

cards.headline: Hundreds of flights cancelled and public transport disrupted in Belgium during strike against austerity measures

pages.text: A strike by air traffic controllers has cancelled hundreds of flights and severely disrupted public transport across Belgium. All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem and at Charleroi, the base for low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. At Brussels Airport, no flights are scheduled to take off or land between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT). In the capital, Brussels, underground services have also been halted as tens of thousands of people joined a protest march. Demonstrators in Brussels rallied to oppose approximately €10 billion in proposed spending cuts, carrying placards with messages such as “Rent is eating into our wages” and “The rich earn more, the workers pay more.” Clashes occurred between protesters and riot police, who responded with water cannons, tear gas, and charges as a car burned and officers made arrests.

The protests come as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with coalition allies regarding a budget intended to cut borrowing costs. De Wever has set a year-end deadline for coalition partners to sign off on the cuts and has warned that the government could collapse if negotiations fail. The planned savings are opposed by protesters who argue that high energy costs, inflation, and shrinking purchasing power mean the cuts could place an unfair burden on the lowest-paid while undermining employment support, help for families, and social security. De Wever met with King Philippe to provide an update on the strained talks over Belgium’s 2027 budget; the King declined his resignation, allowing De Wever more time to negotiate.

Travelers have reported significant confusion and lack of notice regarding the disruptions. One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she discovered there were no flights only upon arriving at the airport. At Charleroi, all flights were shown as “scheduled” regardless of their actual arrival or departure times. Florence Faure, a French passenger who arrived in Brussels from Beijing, reported that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport was cancelled, noting that she did not collect her luggage because it was intended to continue to Paris. Philippe Naime, a teacher, was among the tens of thousands participating in the protest march in Brussels.

cards.headline: Twenty-nine bodies recovered after boat carrying mourners capsizes in Nigeria

pages.text: Search and rescue teams in Nigeria are searching for survivors after a boat carrying mourners traveling to a funeral capsized on November 20, 2026. A spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC that 29 bodies have been recovered and 50 people have been rescued so far. Police spokesperson Musa Mohammed stated the boat was traveling from the Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems. Mohammed added that passengers allegedly asked the boat operator to steer toward land, but he declined, leading to the accident. In response, the government has ordered stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.

Survivors described a scene of panic as they struggled to stay afloat while waiting for emergency services. Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News that while swimming, people were dragging her to the bottom, and she bit one woman to save herself. Another survivor, Tari Samuel, said that while they lost money, phones, and other belongings, he and his siblings are alive. Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns regarding the use of untrained boat operators and passengers traveling without life jackets, noting that some individuals believe familiarity with river areas and swimming skills should replace basic safety precautions.

cards.headline: City of Mississauga implements hiring restrictions effective immediately

pages.text: The City of Mississauga is implementing hiring restrictions, effective immediately, as part of a directive to achieve a zero per cent tax increase for the 2027 and 2028 city budgets. Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo issued the directive to staff during the inaugural council meeting, one week after officially taking on his new role. One of Tedjo's campaign promises was to implement a property tax freeze for his first two years as mayor, and his first task involves drafting the 2027 budget. A spokesperson for the city stated the restrictions are set to be in place until at least March 2027. The city clarified that the policy is not a hiring freeze, as certain positions may still be approved for hire if they receive the necessary authorization.

The restrictions pause all internal and external hiring, which includes appointments, transfers, and contract extensions. Under the new policy, department heads who wish to pursue any new hiring must first obtain approval from either the relevant commissioner or the city manager. According to a city spokesperson, senior staff and the Mayor’s office are working together to develop a plan to meet the zero per cent tax increase goal for the upcoming budget cycles.

cards.headline: Exhibition at London’s Royal Academy of Arts re-examines Peggy Guggenheim’s 18-month London gallery

pages.text: A new exhibition at London’s Royal Academy of Arts, titled “Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector,” uses more than 80 artworks and archival artifacts to re-examine a pivotal 18-month period in the life of art collector Peggy Guggenheim. The show, which runs through March 14, 2027, argues that Guggenheim’s prewar London venture has been unfairly overshadowed by her later fame and sensationalized personal life. Between January 1938 and June 1939, Guggenheim operated a short-lived gallery called Guggenheim Jeune in a modest storefront on London’s Cork Street. During those 18 months, the gallery held 21 exhibitions that introduced skeptical British audiences to radical European modernism and established the foundation for one of the 20th century’s most influential art collections.

Co-curators of the exhibition suggest that Guggenheim’s individual contributions to the art world are often undervalued. Gražina Subelytė, a curator at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice and a co-curator of the London exhibition, told the BBC that Guggenheim has been underrated, noting that public discussion often focuses on her relationships and the advisors who helped her make decisions rather than her own groundbreaking work. Simon Grant, the exhibition's co-curator, told the BBC that Guggenheim's early experience volunteering at New York’s avant-garde, woman-owned Sunwise Turn Bookshop showed her how a woman could be creative and independent, helping her escape upper-class conventions. Born in New York in 1898, Guggenheim grew up on the fringes of wealth after her father, Benjamin Guggenheim, squandered much of the family fortune before dying on the Titanic in 1912.

The exhibition also explores how Guggenheim's views on abstraction and modern art were shaped by her interactions with major creative figures. During a trip to Paris, Irish playwright Samuel Beckett urged her to treat contemporary art as a “living thing,” according to the BBC. Additionally, the Guardian reports that Marcel Duchamp tutored her on the nuances of surrealism and abstraction. These influences helped shape the collector who would later become synonymous with her palazzo art museum on Venice’s Grand Canal.

cards.headline: Soudah Waterfall becomes Saudi Arabia’s second Ramsar wetland

pages.text: Soudah Waterfall has been added to the Ramsar List of Wetlands of International Importance, making it the second site in Saudi Arabia to receive the designation. The National Center for Wildlife and Soudah Development announced that the site, located in the Aseer highlands, has gained this international recognition for its environmental importance. The designation is part of broader efforts to protect ecologically significant landscapes under the Kingdom's Vision 2030 initiative. The Ramsar List recognizes wetlands globally that are considered vital for their ecological value.

Known locally as Wadi Al-Aziza, the site spans approximately 30 hectares and is centered on a 600-meter rocky gorge fed by perennial springs and pools. Perched more than 2,400 meters above sea level in the Soudah highlands, the year-round cascade is a rarity in Saudi Arabia, where permanent mountain waterways are uncommon. The landscape is shaped by moisture from seasonal southwestern monsoon winds, which creates wet habitats and greenery that contrast with the region's typically arid environments.

Scientists consider the area a biodiversity hotspot because it sits where the Paleotropical and Afrotropical floristic zones overlap. This intersection supports a diverse mix of plant and animal life, including rare and endemic species. Beyond its ecology, the surrounding mountains contain historical traces, such as traditional agricultural terraces and the Abo Sarrah Palaces, which date back more than 1,000 years.

cards.headline: Magnetic fields may power stellar winds, challenging previous theories of how stars spread life-essential elements

pages.text: An international team of astronomers has imaged the red giant star Mira in unprecedented detail, revealing that strong magnetic fields may shape and power stellar winds. This finding challenges the long-held belief that these winds are powered solely by starlight pushing on dust grains in a star's outer atmosphere. Because stellar winds are responsible for blowing off a star's outer layers to spread elements like carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen through the Milky Way, this discovery alters the understood process by which the building blocks of new stars, planets, and life are distributed through space. The study, published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics, focused on Mira, a star located 330 light years from Earth in the constellation Cetus the Whale. Mira is older, bigger, and brighter than the sun, but cooler, providing scientists with a real-time glimpse into the potential future of our own star.

The research was conducted by an international team led by Wouter Vlemmings and Miora Andriantsaralaza, both from Chalmers University of Technology. Using the ALMA telescope in Chile, the team captured high-detail images that suggest magnetic fields play a more significant role in stellar wind dynamics than previously thought. Wouter Vlemmings, a professor at the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology, stated that the results change a fundamental part of the origin story regarding the atoms that make up life. While astronomers previously believed starlight provided the necessary push for dust grains to create stellar winds, the observations of Mira indicate that magnetic fields are also a driving force.

cards.headline: Ontario minister defends not initially cutting off career college with skyrocketing OSAP use

pages.text: Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn defended the Ontario government's decision not to initially cut off a career college from the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) despite a massive increase in student financial aid usage. This spring, the ministry made six career colleges ineligible for OSAP due to concerns regarding what it called “high-risk” admissions practices. Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows those six schools saw the number of students receiving OSAP increase between approximately 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25. However, the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among those six schools, even though its OSAP usage grew by 3,000 per cent during that same period.

At one of its four campuses in the Greater Toronto Area, the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology saw OSAP use increase by nearly 6,000 per cent. In 2021-22, the college had 562 students accessing OSAP; three years later, that number reached 17,157. Minister Quinn stated the college avoided the initial funding cuts because the data the ministry was receiving was “evolving.” Quinn said that once the ministry received data showing the situation was “worse than what we initially thought,” the government implemented a pause on OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions. Quinn explained the system-wide pause was intended to understand the impact on all institutions and ensure no other schools like the ones identified had “fallen through the cracks.”

Liberal critic Tyler Watt criticized the ministry's timing, stating the government did not stop the growth at the school until the system-wide OSAP pause was implemented. Watt said, “So either you didn't catch it, despite all these, all these inspections you're bragging about, or you did catch it and you chose to do nothing about it.” The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

cards.headline: President Mahama visits filmmaker Chris Hesse to recount efforts to save Ghana's historical film archives

pages.text: President John Mahama visited veteran filmmaker and photographer Chris Hesse, the former personal cinematographer to Ghana's first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, to recount their past collaboration to prevent the destruction of the country's historical film archives. During the visit, Mahama credited Hesse with the restoration of some of Ghana's earliest historical footage, including films from the era of Dr Kwame Nkrumah, through digitization efforts intended to make the materials available for future generations.

Mahama stated that their efforts to protect the archives began during his tenure as Deputy Minister of Communications. He recalled that Hesse showed him deteriorating and mouldy film reels at the Information Services Department. While they attempted to retrieve some films, Mahama said others could not be saved due to the extent of the damage. Hesse later informed Mahama that well-preserved copies of the films were being held at a Rank Xerox laboratory in London.

The preservation of these films faced a crisis when Rank Xerox threatened to dispose of them due to unpaid bills. Mahama recounted that the government owed the company approximately £10,000 at the time, and the company threatened to dump the films at the embassy if the debt was not settled. Mahama said he made a case for payment, which resulted in the outstanding amount being settled and the government making annual payments to maintain the films.

cards.headline: Israel seeks to hold Palestinian student in administrative detention without trial

pages.text: Israeli authorities are seeking to hold Mahdi Tounsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, in administrative detention without trial. After the police's original arrest warrant for Tounsi expired, authorities submitted an order for administrative detention—a process allowing for detention without charge—signed by Defence Minister Israel Katz. Tounsi, an East Jerusalem resident, was taken from his dorm room on 8 November. He has been held without charge for more than two weeks. During a court hearing via video link on 19 November, Tounsi appeared with visible facial bruising, lacked his necessary glasses, and had his hair and beard shaved. Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in his dorm, in a patrol car, and at a police station, according to Israeli media reports.

Interrogators questioned Tounsi regarding his activism with Standing Together and Ir Amim, two Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups. Both organizations have called for his immediate release. Standing Together warned that security agencies are being used to silence political activity and critical speech, stating that the university should intervene to ensure a fair judicial process. Ir Amim described Tounsi as a partner in movements that bring Palestinians and Israelis together and expressed serious concerns regarding his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process. Israeli professors, students, and rights activists are also calling for his release.

The detention occurs amid what has been described as a campaign of delegitimization against Palestinian citizens of Israel. Following an election in which Palestinian votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority, Netanyahu and his allies used false accusations of mass fraud to attempt to maintain power, though Israel’s election commission validated the results. Netanyahu has faced accusations of fostering racist rhetoric and politicizing security institutions in campaigns against Palestinian-led parties.

cards.headline: Visual cortex plays active role in transforming threatening experiences into lasting fear memories

pages.text: Researchers at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston have discovered that the brain's visual cortex—the area typically responsible for processing sight—plays an active role in determining whether a threatening experience becomes embedded as a lasting fear memory. While research into fear memory has traditionally focused on emotion-associated brain regions like the amygdala, these findings suggest the visual system helps shape how these memories persist. This mechanism could offer new ways to prevent persistent fear and treat conditions such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and anxiety disorders, which can occur when fear memories become overly persistent.

The study, titled “Sensory cortical disinhibition underlies long-term fear memory in humans,” was published Nov. 14 in Nature Communications. Led by Wen Li, Ph.D., the John S. Dunn professor in the Louis A. Faillace, MD, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at McGovern Medical School, the research utilized a combination of neuroimaging, artificial intelligence, and noninvasive brain stimulation. The researchers also discovered that noninvasive brain stimulation can interrupt the process of transforming threatening experiences into lasting fear memories.

cards.headline: Black River First Nation plans high-purity quartz mining in Manitoba

pages.text: Black River First Nation is planning a sand mining operation on its land near Vivian, Manitoba, to harvest high-purity quartz for a solar panel manufacturing facility. Sheldon Kent, chief of the Black River First Nation located on the east shore of Lake Winnipeg, announced the partnership with mining company Sio Silica during a news conference with the Southern Chiefs' Organization. The proposed project involves just over 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of land that the community purchased a few years ago due to its economic potential. Kent stated that the community intends to proceed with the project regardless of whether the provincial government grants a mining licence, asserting that the First Nation has the jurisdiction and right to use its own land.

Kent described the environmental plan for the Sio Silica project as sustainable, workable, and safe, noting that the community would not participate if the operation were destructive to their land. While Kent expressed that the ideal scenario involves the Manitoba NDP government granting a licence, he maintained that the First Nation will move forward with or without provincial approval. Sio Silica has promised a $125M sand-storage facility in Churchill, Manitoba, if a mining licence is approved.

cards.headline: Ghana secures approximately 6.5 million forest carbon credits with potential US$68 million value

pages.text: Ghana has obtained approximately 6.5 million carbon credits through the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions (ART), a milestone that could generate nearly US$68 million from the sale of these credits. The country is the first in Africa and the third globally, following Guyana and Costa Rica, to achieve this under the REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard (TREES). Each credit represents one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in verified emission reductions achieved between 2017 and 2021 through forest landscape restoration and measures to prevent deforestation and forest degradation. Forestry Commission Chief Executive Dr. Hugh Brown stated that these credits were earned through measurable conservation results that were achieved, measured, reported, and independently validated, rather than being simply allocated to the country.

The Forestry Commission noted that while credits have been issued, the country has yet to receive the corresponding revenue. Dr. Brown emphasized the distinction between the issuance of verified credits and the actual receipt of funds. Currently, buyers including participants in the LEAF Coalition have committed to purchasing four million credits valued at approximately US$43 million. The remaining 2.5 million credits are available for further transactions and could potentially generate an additional US$25 million. Under the program's benefit-sharing arrangement, forest-fringe communities, farmers, and traditional authorities are expected to receive 46 per cent of the proceeds.

cards.headline: Egypt and Iraq pledge closer energy and military ties during Iraqi Prime Minister's first Cairo visit

pages.text: Egypt's President Abdel Fattah El Sisi and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi discussed expanding cooperation in energy, investment, trade, and military affairs during Al Zaidi's first official visit to Cairo. The discussions, which covered bilateral ties and regional crises, coincided with the fourth session of the Egyptian-Iraqi joint higher committee in the New Administrative Capital. Following the committee meeting, Al Zaidi and Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly were expected to sign agreements covering finance, planning, agriculture, transport, trade, and industry, according to Iraq's Trade Ministry.

During the visit, Iraqi officials stated the two countries were discussing Iraq supplying Egypt with approximately 10 million barrels of crude, though the delivery period was not specified. The talks included exploring export routes that avoid the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq and other Gulf oil-producing states have sought alternative routes to the strait after Iran effectively shut the waterway following US-Israeli attacks in February. Iraq's oil exports, which represent more than 90 per cent of its budget, fell from 3.36 million barrels per day in February to 131,000 barrels per day in April, before recovering to about 2.7 million barrels per day as Baghdad utilized alternative routes, such as a pipeline to Turkey, according to Iraq's oil ministry.

Al Zaidi, a 41-year-old businessman who became Iraq's youngest Prime Minister in May, said Iraq seeks closer consultation with Egypt to prevent renewed regional escalation. President El Sisi noted that both sides agreed to strengthen political consultation mechanisms to address regional challenges. Additionally, El Sisi stated that both leaders reject attempts to undermine the freedom and security of navigation in the Red Sea, the Bab Al Mandeb strait, and the Gulf.

cards.headline: Yale study finds sensory neurons adjust to learned preferences in roundworms

pages.text: A Yale study published in the journal Current Biology reveals that sensory neurons—specialized nerve cells that transmit environmental information from the senses to the brain—play a more complex role in behavior than previously understood. Researchers found that these neurons can adjust their responses to environmental changes based on an animal's learned preferences, providing insight into how experience shapes how a nervous system transforms sensory information into signals to achieve goals. To investigate this, the research team used Caenorhabditis elegans, a type of roundworm, to observe how sensory landscapes are shaped by memory.

The research team trained the roundworms to prefer specific temperature conditions by using food rewards. Researchers constructed a gradient containing different temperatures in various spots. After placing the worms on this gradient, the animals moved toward the temperature they had learned to prefer. Daniel Colón-Ramos, the Dorys McConnell Duberg Professor of Neuroscience and Cell Biology at Yale School of Medicine and the study's lead author, stated that the worms remember the temperature at which they were under favorable conditions while eating and return to that temperature. The study noted that unexpected activity occurred deep inside the worm's nervous system during this process.

cards.headline: Terrace, British Columbia, elects its second-ever Indigenous city councillor

pages.text: Nikki Villeneuve, a print shop owner of Nisga'a and Gitxsan heritage, was elected to the Terrace city council on Oct. 17, becoming the second Indigenous person to hold the role of councillor in the city's history. The election comes despite a significant Indigenous presence in the northwest British Columbia region; 2021 census data shows Indigenous people made up nearly 22 per cent of Terrace's population and approximately 25 per cent of the wider Terrace census area.

Villeneuve grew up on the Gitanyow reserve, formerly known as Kitwancool, a community of about 400 people located approximately 90 kilometres northeast of Terrace. She moved to Terrace 17 years ago. Villeneuve stated that her perspective is influenced by her upbringing in a community where residents supported one another. The Terrace city council held its inaugural meeting in November.

cards.headline: Residents of Sonitra Adekopa, Ghana, report health threats from refuse dump

pages.text: Residents of Sonitra Adekopa in the Ga West Municipal Assembly are raising concerns over a massive refuse dump located in the middle of a residential area. They describe the site as a serious threat to public health, safety, and general well-being. The dumpsite has reportedly subjected the community to persistent foul odours, environmental pollution, and the potential outbreak of diseases. Residents claim the situation has deteriorated over time, forcing some neighbours to abandon their homes to find healthier and more comfortable environments. An Onua News team visited the site and observed what they described as deplorable and unsanitary conditions at the dumpsite.

Community members allege that individuals who speak out against the refuse dump face intimidation and physical attacks. Residents claim that suspected land guards, known locally as goro boys, allegedly attack outspoken residents in their homes, which they say has created an atmosphere of fear and panic. Regarding official responses, residents claim that repeated complaints to the Ga West Municipal Assembly have yielded no meaningful results. Attempts to secure an interview with the Municipal Chief Executive for Ga West, Desmond Sowah, have been unsuccessful for nearly three months. Residents are appealing to the Ga West Municipal Assembly and other relevant authorities to intervene, clear the refuse, and implement sustainable sanitation measures to prevent a public health crisis.

cards.headline: Al Ain Museum exhibition explores 3,000 years of water management through aflaj systems

pages.text: The Al Ain Museum will open an exhibition titled “Aflaj – the life-giving veins of the oasis” on November 27, exploring nearly 3,000 years of water management and the communities that developed around it. The exhibition features a drawing made more than five decades ago by the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the UAE Founding Father, which illustrates the route of a falaj. This drawing, published by Al Ittihad newspaper on August 6, 1972, traces the underground channels used to irrigate many of the city's date palm groves. A falaj is an engineering system of underground channels that has sustained Al Ain's oases for generations.

cards.headline: Scientists observe vaporized rock around a massive young star

pages.text: Researchers have observed titanium oxide in gas form around a massive, young star, marking the first time scientists have determined the composition of solid materials outside of our solar system without collecting physical samples. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the team studied the disk of Orion Source I, a massive, young star located in a dusty cloud behind the Orion Nebula. University of Florida Associate Professor of Astronomy Adam Ginsburg, Ph.D., identified the system and developed some of the techniques used for the analysis. This discovery provides a method to understand the makeup of solid objects in space remotely, a task previously limited to materials brought to Earth-based laboratories.

The discovery overcomes a fundamental limitation in space observation. While scientists can analyze the composition of gases in space through spectroscopy—a method where gas molecules provide specific spectral data—solid objects are much harder to identify. When observing rocks in space, scientists typically only see the light the objects reflect, which does not allow for identification of their specific composition. To study solids, researchers generally must bring them to a physical lab, blast them with heat to evaporate the material, and then use a spectrograph to measure the resulting gas molecules. In the case of Orion Source I, the researchers found a natural version of this process, where the environment itself evaporates the material for analysis.

cards.headline: Four historical parkas found at a British Columbia thrift store may return to Nunavut

pages.text: Mike Williams, a retired IT worker in Kamloops, British Columbia, is attempting to return four historical parkas to Nunavut after discovering them at a local thrift store. Williams found the garments at a Value Village in mid-October, including one parka bearing the name of Selena ‘Kublu’ Tucktoo of Taloyoak, Nunavut. He initially intended to resell the items but changed his plans after learning about their history. Tucktoo, who made the parka when she was in her early 20s, stated she and other seamstresses in her community created the garments for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games held in Anchorage, Alaska.

cards.headline: Bangladesh garment workers to receive rice at Tk30 per kilogram under government program

pages.text: A special government program in Bangladesh will provide rice to garment workers at a rate of Tk30 per kilogram. This initiative comes as the country's garment industry, which generated $38.82 billion in 2025, remains a central part of the global supply chain. While the industry is often described as an economic miracle of globalization and free trade, the necessity of this rice program suggests that workers producing this wealth cannot afford to feed themselves without state intervention.

cards.headline: Webb telescope observations of Cassiopeia A remnant suggest star underwent dramatic change before explosion

pages.text: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has provided high-resolution, mid-infrared observations of the Cassiopeia A (Cas A) supernova remnant, revealing details that help astronomers track the structure and evolution of the original star. The data supports a scenario where the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Supernova remnants are clouds of gas and dust left behind after a massive star explodes; these materials eventually seed the formation of new stars and planets.

The observations help chronicle how stars evolve through a process of nuclear fusion. Stars begin as molecular clouds of hydrogen gas and cosmic dust that collapse under gravity to form protostars. As gravity increases pressure, hydrogen fuses into helium, turning protostars into full-fledged stars. When hydrogen in the core is exhausted, the core contracts and heats, causing helium to fuse into heavier elements. This cycle repeats, creating multiple shells of different elements—with heavier elements in the core and lighter elements in surrounding layers—that serve as a record of the star's history. When the star eventually goes supernova, these elements scatter into space and condense into dust grains.

cards.headline: Two monkey brain regions influence choices differently using the same information

pages.text: Researchers from the University of Chicago, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and Cornell University have found that two distinct brain regions in monkeys influence decision-making in different ways, even when processing the exact same information. The study, published in Nature Neuroscience, addresses a fundamental question in neuroscience regarding why the brain is organized into specialized areas if many different regions can represent the same information about what an animal sees or does. The findings suggest that while different areas may hold the same data, they organize that information differently to prepare it for different mental computations and behaviors.

To test how these differences in information formatting affect behavior, the researchers trained two rhesus macaques to make decisions by combining two types of information: the direction of moving dots on a screen and the rewards associated with different choices. The study focused on the contributions of the middle temporal area (MT) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) to the decision-making process. Senior author Cohen told Medical Xpress that the project aimed to determine if the way brain areas organize information provides insight into, or determines, how they contribute to behavior.

cards.headline: Valentine gold mine expansion in Newfoundland to increase production

pages.text: The Valentine gold mine, the largest in Atlantic Canada, is undergoing a $436-million expansion intended to increase gold production by approximately 25 per cent. This project is creating an unincorporated, unnamed community in central Newfoundland that functions like a small town. Jason Cyr, the VP of Canadian operations for mine owner Equinox Gold, stated that the site currently has about a thousand employees at one time, though the total number reaches approximately 2,000 because workers operate on a schedule of two weeks on and two weeks off.

The unnamed site's population is greater than that of all the closest communities combined. Phase 2 construction is scheduled to start in the new year and is expected to bring more long-term jobs to the region. The site is located approximately three hours from the Trans Canada Highway toward Buchans. Access involves traveling over dirt roads that can turn into mud during rain or create dust when dry, including a particularly twisty section known by employees as The Snake.

cards.headline: Archaeological research suggests Iron Age British ruler Verica may have been a woman

pages.text: New research from Bournemouth University suggests that Verica, an influential Iron Age British ruler long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe with lands extending across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. This finding challenges longstanding assumptions regarding the political influence of women in early British history and suggests that 19th-century classical historians incorrectly identified the ruler's gender due to a patriarchal mindset.

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that Verica was indisputably female. Russell points to the name Verica itself as evidence, noting that it ends in the letter “a,” a feature common among female names of that period. Verica played a pivotal role in the events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome to seek assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal to the Emperor was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history. The research suggests Verica was critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD.

cards.headline: Newly discovered viruses suggest complex evolutionary link between viruses and cellular compartments

pages.text: Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that may explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding, published in Nature Communications, reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and encapsulins—tiny protein compartments found inside cells. This discovery challenges the conventional scientific belief that these cellular compartments evolved from viruses, suggesting instead a more complicated relationship where viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The connection centers on proteins that fold into a specific three-dimensional structure called the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are present in both viruses and encapsulins. The newly identified viruses possess smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. Because they exhibit characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, these viruses may serve as evolutionary intermediates between the two.

Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared and offer clues regarding the development of some of life's earliest biological structures. The discovery may also have implications for biotechnology and suggests that viruses might possess biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.
